doc.title: John Bunch interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

title: Personalities of Goodman, Rich and Bennett; precision and slow tempos
summary: Goodman's moods, Rich's tantrums yet gentle featuring of him, and Bennett's demanding precision.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: Benny Goodman was, you just can’t explain him. You never could understand what he wanted sometimes. And then he could turn and be an absolute dream guy, just the life of the party. He could turn out to be, tell jokes and if you told him a joke and he was in the right mood he’d collapse on the floor practically laughing. You know he could be just a really wonderful guy. But then he could turn around at a rehearsal and just practically insult a person, you know insult a musician. You know he’d give you a look like, a terrible look, he’d look you in the eye and go — as if he hated you. I got sort of used to it after a few years. And Buddy Rich was always very nice to me and always let me take solos and feature me and all that stuff. But he was really tough on the young musicians. I thought unreasonably so. He’d have tirades. He’d have great temper tantrums, almost like a little, child, a spoiled child. And it was sort of embarrassing to be there and witness that. I mean but he’d turn around the play the drums so great, I mean so exciting. You could hardly play with him you know. And when he’d feature me he would play so soft, as if it was my band. Always. When he’d feature that one tune he’d feature me on, it was so delicate. And he’d turn right around. This guy that had this temper, you know it’s hard to figure out. And in Tony Bennett’s case, I think in that case it was more familiarity. I just was so close to him all the time. A pianist that plays for a singer like that, every, it’s so professional, I can’t tell you, it’s got to be exactly. It can’t be just sort of exact. The tempos have to be on the button. And the bass player, if he — he can’t be faking. It’s got to be every note it’s got to be exactly what the music says. It’s a different kind of music from jazz you know. Maybe it’s different now. He does have a, he works with a trio now. But see when I was with him it was a big orchestra, a great big orchestra. Even symphonies sometimes. And anyhow he wanted it just so. And the slow tempos were so slow. That takes a great concentration for a musician to play slow. It’s not just concentrating to play fast. Slow is also very difficult.
Sometimes it’s harder than playing fast, isn’t it?

Yes almost. Because you have to, you can’t dare take a drink before the show. At least I had to quit all that, no more, not even a martini before dinner or anything like that, just nothing. Because it took too much concentration. And then after a few years of that I finally got to where I decided it was time to leave. So anyhow, that’s the sort of story that I had about those three.
